items.title: ‘A civilisational crisis’: The IISc professor whose AI talk went viral
items.summary: Study maths, learn to think, learn programming or get a job. For a generation of Indian STEM students, that was the script. Now AI may be tearing up that playbook – so how do we adapt to this new world order?. In this conversation, Indulekha Aravind speaks with Dr Prathosh AP, assistant professor in the Department of Electrical Communication Engineering at IISc Bengaluru, whose classroom talk on pedagogy in the age of AI went viral. If our only goal is to improve efficiency and productivity, why work with humans, with our quirks and limitations – why not use AI, rather than people, he asks. What is our “moat”, as humans? What will become of work, as we know it, and the process of learning? Would there be any point in having colleges, classrooms and lectures? And are we having enough conversations about this "civilisational shift” that’s under way? Three of Prathosh’s students, who were in his class the day of his viral lecture and whose questions, in fact, provoked that talk, join him in the studio to explain their anxieties and hopes in this changing world. Prathosh also explains why his inbox flooded, and why he couldn’t sleep. Watch the full conversation. A quarter-century of Modi governance calls for questions and a hamper. To mark the occasion, we have offers for subscribers and other readers .

items.title: What the Gujarat lawyers’ protest reveals about our democracy
items.summary: For the last few days, lawyers across the State of Gujarat have been up in arms against the Rent Control Bill, 2026 (here “up in arms” is used metaphorically, lest the State government rely on this post to slam sedition and UAPA cases against the protesting lawyers or, much worse, the author). Although this post briefly addresses the causes of concern in the proposed Bill, the main aim of this post is to address the assurance advanced by the Advocate General (AG) to the effect that the Bill will never see the light of the day . This post explores, through the assurance advanced by the AG, the reality of the relationship between the State government and the Governor - a topic which has received considerable engagement from constitutional lawyers as well as courts in the recent past. Why are the lawyers protesting? The protest is directed against the Rent Control Bill, 2026, which seeks to take away the jurisdiction of small causes courts to decide rent disputes and instead vests the revenue authorities such as mamlatdar or deputy collector with the jurisdiction to decide these disputes. There are three main objections to this Bill: one constitutional, one practical and one professional. The constitutional objection is based on the settled principle of separation of powers. The power to decide disputes is a judicial function which cannot be vested in a purely administrative authorities which are part of the executive wing of the State. Recall the long line of judgments by the Supreme Court that require even tribunals - which are quasi-judicial bodies - to have a judicial member along with a technical member in order to ensure proper administration of justice. There is no reason whatsoever to depart from that position in this case and vest a judicial, or even a quasi-judicial authority, in an executive office. The second and practical objection is on the basis that the offices of mamlatdars and deputy collectors are already overburdened with administrative duties. Vesting the responsibility of resolving disputes will result in delays in administration of justice and resolution of such disputes. Therefore, the concern is also whether this change will actually expedite dispute resolution and, if not, then what necessitated the change. items.title: Kerala High Court comes to aid of principal denied entry to school for wearing churidar
items.summary: The Kerala High Court recently directed the police to ensure that a headmistress of a high school in Kottarakkara is allowed to enter the educational institution freely after she was allegedly stopped at the gate for wearing a churidar [Sindhu S Nair v Secretary, General Education Department & ors] Justice PV Kunhikrishnan said that a person's choice of attire cannot be dictated by another person or by societal customs unless such a restriction has the backing of law. The Court emphasised that when such dictates are issued against the individual choices of a citizen, it is the duty of the law-enforcing authority to take appropriate legal steps. " What dress one wears is ordinarily a matter of personal choice of every citizen of this country. No one or society as a whole can dictate how a citizen should dress without the backing of the law. This is a part of the fundamental rights of every citizen, " the Court said. It added that clothes are an expression of culture, comfort, and individual choice which cannot be used to measure a person's worth or dignity. The Court declared that a citizen's attire is her choice and cannot be restricted by any societal customs. " I declare that a citizen's attire is his/her choice, and nobody can insist that it conform to society's customs, nor can anybody dictate that it be in a manner acceptable to society, especially when no law backs it." Justice PV Kunhikrishnan Though the dispute appears to be a simple issue of whether a headmistress could wear a churidar instead of a saree during working hours, it raises broader questions concerning the dignity and autonomy of a woman, the Court SAID. " The Constitution does not make a woman's dignity contingent on her conformity with another person’s preferred mode of attire. Dress is a personal choice ," it added. The Court further emphasised that the dignity or cultural significance attached to an attire is for the person wearing it to decide and cannot be imposed according to societal preferences. " No one can restrict it, and no one can dictate which dress an individual must wear. The dignity and cultural tradition of an attire should be decided by the person concerned, not by society, " the Court said. items.title: P&H High Court initiates contempt case against The Hindu, Dainik Bhaskar over Dera Sacha Sauda propaganda ads
items.summary: The Punjab and Haryana High Court has initiated suo motu contempt of court proceedings against the editors-in-chief and publishers of The Hindu and Dainik Bhaskar for publishing Dera Sacha Sauda advertisements claiming that its chief, Gurmeet Ram Rahim Singh, was being targeted as part of a conspiracy. The matter was today listed before a bench of Justice Vinod S Bhardwaj and Justice Ravinder Malik . The Court listed it for consideration on November 25. Gurmeet Ram Rahim Singh is currently serving a 20-year sentence for raping his two disciples. His appeal challenging the conviction and sentence is pending before the High Court. The High Court in 2024 and in March this year had acquitted him in two different murders cases. On September 12, the newspapers published a front-page advertisement which claimed that there was a conspiracy against Ram Rahim. The Hindu later issued a public apology for publishing the advertisement following public backlash. The issue has now got revived in view of the suo motu contempt proceedings initiated on an order passed by Justice Subhas Mehla who said the newspaper advertisements insinuated that courts were a party to the alleged conspiracy. The judge said that the advertisements were an attempt to mobilize public opinion and influence the judicial process, adding that such action directly obstructs the administration of justice. "On a prima facie consideration of the aforesaid advertisement publications, this Court is of the view that the contents thereof may have the tendency to scandalise or lower the authority of this Court," the judge added. Thus, he opined that the matter warrants examination of the publications in contempt jurisdiction. "Accordingly, this Court takes suo motu cognizance of criminal contempt under Article 215 of the Constitution of India read with Section 2(c)(i), 2(c)(iii) and 15(1) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971," Justice Mehla said in the reference order passed last month.

items.title: CJI Surya Kant to attend NLSIU convocation on October 17
items.summary: Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant will attend the 34th annual convocation of the National Law School of India University (NLSIU), Bengaluru on October 17. The convocation will be held from 11 am to 1 pm at the Jnana Jyoti Auditorium on Palace Road, Bengaluru. Justice Kant, who is the Chancellor of NLSIU, will preside over the ceremony, the University said in an invitation circulated to invitees. The convocation comes after NLSIU had earlier cancelled the ceremony scheduled for September 12 after issuing a notice announcing that no convocation would be held for the 2026 batch due to "unavoidable circumstances" and that students would be conferred their degrees in absentia. The cancellation came amid a controversy over the proposed presence of CJI Kant and Bar Council of India (BCI) Chairman Manan Kumar Mishra at the ceremony. More than 700 current students, graduating students and alumni had objected to their participation. The development followed a separate controversy at NALSAR University of Law, Hyderabad, where students had opposed the proposed presence of CJI Kant at their convocation. The issue escalated on August 13 when the BCI directed State Bar Councils to halt the enrolment of NALSAR's graduating batch, after which the direction was withdrawn within hours . NLSIU students and alumni subsequently expressed solidarity with the NALSAR students and criticised the BCI's action. On August 15, over 700 members of the NLSIU community signed a statement objecting to BCI chairperson Manan Kumar Mishra and CJI Surya Kant attending NLSIU's convocation. According to reports, CJI Kant subsequently met NLSIU students to hear their concerns. Students were later asked to vote on whether they would attend a convocation at which the CJI would be present. A majority supported the arrangement, with the understanding that Mishra would not attend. However, the issue resurfaced after students were subsequently asked to publicly invite the CJI to the ceremony. The graduating batch did not agree to the additional demand, following which the September 12 convocation was cancelled. NLSIU's governing bodies later approved October 17 as the new date for the convocation. Students were given the option of receiving their degrees in person at the ceremony or in absentia.

items.title: NCLT orders winding up of 14 Popular Finance-linked entities; asks liquidator to trace money, recover assets
items.summary: The National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) at Kochi has ordered the winding up of 14 entities linked to the Popular Finance Group and directed the liquidators to trace money collected from the public and identify assets acquired using such funds. A Bench of Judicial Member Vinay Goel and Technical Member Ravichandran Ramasamy passed the batch of orders on October 6 on petitions moved by the Union government through the Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO). The 14 entities comprise companies and limited liability partnerships belonging to the Popular Finance Group. The tribunal issued substantially similar directions in the winding-up proceedings and asked liquidators to examine the SFIO investigation report and determine where money collected from members of the public ultimately went. “ Examine the SFIO Investigation Report and other material available on record and trace the flow and end-use of funds collected from the public, ” the tribunal ruled. The liquidators have also been directed to identify properties and assets acquired from such funds and initiate appropriate proceedings for their recovery, restoration or protection for the benefit of the entities and their stakeholders. They have further been asked to invite, verify and adjudicate claims from creditors, depositors, investors and other stakeholders, besides seeking information and assistance from the SFIO, Registrar of Companies, banks, financial institutions and other investigating agencies. The directions assume significance since the SFIO investigation found that the Popular Finance Group had mobilised approximately ₹4,700 crore from members of the public. Of this, around ₹829.31 crore was attributed to the companies and LLPs covered by the investigation. According to the SFIO, the Group raised funds through fixed, recurring and savings deposits, capital contributions and debentures. It alleged that the money was routed among various group concerns and that funds collected from the public were ultimately used for purposes including the personal use of directors and designated partners. The investigation also alleged that the Group offered interest rates ranging between 9 percent and 18.18 percent to attract investors and projected its gold-loan operations as the face of its business. items.summary: The State government is duty-bound to ensure that public recruitment examinations are conducted impartially and without malpractices, the Bombay High Court observed on Wednesday while hearing a plea regarding ongoing student agitations in Pune [Amit Supekar & Anr v. State of Maharashtra & Ors.] A division bench comprising Chief Justice Mahesh Chandra Tripathi and Justice Advait Sethna made these observations while hearing a write petition filed over the ongoing agitations in Pune regarding the Maharashtra Public Service Commission (MPSC) drug inspector recruitment examinations. “The State has to give an assurance that whatever examinations are conducted, is impartial, fair and there should be no malpractices. Chief Justice Mahesh Chandra Tripathi and Justice Advait Sethna The Court highlighted the responsibility of State authorities to ensure recruitment happens. “The onus is on the State to ensure recruitment happens and it should be streamlined.” The bench also said that students have a right to agitate if they are aggrieved. “If students are agitated, there are some things that need to be considered. items.title: Supreme Court acquits government employee who spent 4 years in jail in 16-year-old corruption case
items.summary: Sixteen years after he was accused of demanding a ₹5,000 bribe, and long after he finished serving his four-year prison sentence, a former Jharkhand government employee was recently acquitted by the Supreme Court in a corruption case [ Ajit Kumar v. State of Jharkhand ]. A Bench of Justices Ujjal Bhuyan and Atul S Chandurkar set aside the conviction of the appellant, one Ajit Kumar, holding that the prosecution failed to prove the demand and acceptance of any bribe. Justices Ujjal Bhuyan and Atul S Chandurkar Notably, when the top court first took up his plea on July 24, 2026, Kumar had already undergone the entire four-year rigorous imprisonment term and paid the ₹10,000 fine earlier imposed on him. However, his counsel informed the Court that Kumar wished to fight the appeal to its logical conclusion to clear his name and remove the institutional stigma attached to a corruption conviction. The case dates back to April 2010, when a school orderly alleged that Kumar - then working in the District Education Office at Saraikella - demanded money to release his pending salary. He was booked in a corruption case. In February 2021, the Special Judge for the Anti-Corruption Bureau at Chaibasa convicted Kumar and imposed a four-year prison sentence as punishment. The Jharkhand High Court upheld the conviction in July 2022. Following the High Court's dismissal of his appeal, Kumar served out his four-year term of rigorous imprisonment and paid the fine. He subsequently approached the Supreme Court seeking to clear his name. On July 24, when the top court issued notice on his plea, his counsel clarified that despite having already undergone the entire sentence, Kumar wished to pursue the appeal to erase the stigma of conviction. Scrutinising the trial record, the Supreme Court discovered critical gaps in the prosecution's case. The Court highlighted that not a single member of the trap team or any independent witness actually saw Kumar demand or accept the money, as the alleged transaction took place inside his residence without any observers present. The Bench noted that the conviction rested entirely on the uncorroborated testimony of the complainant, while official witnesses admitted they merely signed pre-drafted seizure lists at the behest of vigilance officers. items.title: One Nation, One Election: DMK's P Wilson defends JPC proposal to meet Supreme Court judges
items.summary: The meeting proposed by Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC) examining the One Nation, One Election Bills with Supreme Court judges was done based on a proposal by Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) party MP, JPC member and Senior Advocate P Wilson. The proposed meeting was called off amid objections over the propriety of sitting judges discussing legislation that could later come before the Court for judicial review. However, Wilson has now defended the proposal for such a meeting. "Unfortunately, due to political objections surrounding this meeting, it was decided to call off the meeting because of unnecessary and unfortunate circumstances caused by vested interests," said Wilson in his statement. The JPC is chaired by Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) MP PP Chaudhary. It had proposed an interaction with Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and other Supreme Court judges. The meeting was part of the JPC's consultations on the Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill, 2024 and the Union Territories Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2024. The Bills seek to provide for simultaneous elections to the Lok Sabha, State Assemblies and Union Territory legislatures. The Supreme Court had initially agreed to the interaction, with the offices of the JPC and the CJI exchanging communications on the proposed delegation. The meeting was subsequently called off on October 1, after concerns were raised about sitting judges discussing legislation that could potentially come before the Court. Notably, the proposal had drawn public criticism from Rajya Sabha MP and senior advocate Kapil Sibal , who questioned its constitutional propriety. "This is a joke on the Constitution," said Sibal. items.title: Supreme Court dismisses plea for recitation of Preamble during morning assembly in schools
items.summary: The Supreme Court on Tuesday dismissed a public interest litigation (PIL) seeking directions to formulate a national policy mandating the daily recitation of the Preamble to the Constitution during morning assemblies in schools nationwide [Dheeraj Kumar v. Union of India & Anr]. A Bench of Justices Vikram Nath, Sandeep Mehta and Augustine George Masih refused to entertain the plea, remarking that the Preamble is already part of the foundational school curriculum and is taught to students across the country from Class 6 onwards. Justice Vikram Nath, Justice Sandeep Mehta and Justice Augustine George Masih The PIL was instituted by Dheeraj Kumar, an Assistant Professor at Rajdhani College, Delhi University, through Advocate-on-Record Rohit Kumar. The petitioner sought a writ of mandamus directing the Union Ministry of Education and the Central Board of Secondary Education (CBSE) to frame a nationwide policy framework to promote constitutional literacy among school students. The plea submitted that regular and collective engagement with the Preamble akin to the rendition of the National Anthem during morning prayers would instill foundational values of justice, liberty, equality and fraternity from an early age, in furtherance of the fundamental right to education under Article 21A and fundamental duties under Article 51A(a). To support the prayer, the petition placed reliance on circulars issued by the governments of Rajasthan, Maharashtra and Karnataka, which had previously directed state-run and affiliated schools to have students recite the Preamble during morning assemblies. The petition further cited CBSE's May 2025 circular encouraging daily positive affirmations in assemblies, contending that reciting the Preamble was the ultimate affirmation of civic consciousness. Additional Sessions Judge (ASJ) Saurabh Pratap Singh Laler of the Patiala House Court passed the order. The judge had earlier granted him interim bail for three weeks . The Court had then said that it would observe his conduct before considering his plea for regular bail. Bhardwaj was arrested from Uttar Pradesh on September 5 for allegedly assaulting the father of a Dalit student-activist during the CJP protests at Jantar Mantar in July. He was booked for offences of assault and provisions under the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act [SC/ST Act]. items.title: Supreme Court closes Constitution Bench reference case on legislative privilege and free speech
items.summary: The Supreme Court on Tuesday closed a 2003 case referred to a Constitution Bench to examine the limits of legislative privilege and its interplay with free speech [ N Ravi and others v. Speaker, Legislative Assembly, Chennai and others ]. The Court decided to close the case in view of the fact that the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly had recalled the resolution based on which the case came to be initiated. Therefore, a seven-judge Constitution Bench of Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Aravind Kumar, Prashant Kumar Mishra, Joymalya Bagchi, Vipul M Pancholi, Shree Chandrashekhar and V Mohana closed the matter as infructuous. The Court clarified that the larger questions of law raised in the case remain open but can be examined in future in appropriate proceedings. " The writ petitions are disposed of as having become infructuous. However, the questions of law are kept open to be pursued in future in appropriate proceedings," the Court said. The case dates back to 2003 and arose from privilege proceedings initiated by the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly against journalists of The Hindu by a resolution passed on November 7, 2003. The Assembly had sentenced then Editor N Ravi, Executive Editor Malini Parthasarathy, Publisher S Rangarajan, Chief of Bureau V Jayant and Special Correspondent Radha Venkatesan to 15 days' simple imprisonment for breach of privilege and contempt over an editorial critical of the then State government headed by Chief Minister J Jayalalithaa. The journalists then approached the Supreme Court against the same. The top court stayed their arrest in November 2003. In December 2003, the Court found that the dispute raised substantial questions concerning Article 194(3), which deals with legislative privileges, and its interplay with the freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) and the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 of the Constitution. items.title: Banks can't unilaterally reduce interest on fixed deposits maintained pursuant to court orders: Delhi High Court
items.summary: Banks cannot unilaterally reduce interest on fixed deposits maintained pursuant to court orders without justification, the Delhi High Court recently held [ Natwest Vs Hero Exports ]. A bench of Justices Avneesh Jhingan and Shail Jain passed a ruling to this effect while dismissing an appeal by NatWest Markets PLC against an order requiring it to pay higher interest on a ₹5.89 crore fixed deposit that was being maintained during the pendency of an arbitration dispute. Justice Avneesh Jhingan The dispute arose between Hero Exports and Tiffins Barrytes, Asbestos and Paints Limited. Before arbitration proceedings commenced, Hero Exports moved the High Court under Section 9 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act seeking interim protection. In July 2008, the High Court ordered that ₹8.5 crore lying in Tiffins Barrytes' bank accounts be secured. Of this, ₹5.89 crore was lying with ABN Amro Bank, which later became Royal Bank of Scotland and is now NatWest Markets PLC. The Court subsequently directed that the ₹5.89 crore be kept in a fixed deposit yielding the maximum rate of interest. The deposit earned interest at rates of 7.75 percent, 8.25 percent and 7.75 percent until January 30, 2018. Thereafter, the bank reduced the interest rate to 3.5 per cent. In May 2019, a single-judge of the High Court took exception to the reduction in the interest rate and directed the bank to deposit the entire amount with the Registrar General of the High Court. The judge further ordered that interest from January 30, 2018, should be calculated on the average of the preceding three years' rates. NatWest challenged the order before the High Court's Division Bench, relying on an RBI circular which permits commercial banks to fix their own interest rates on domestic term deposits. It also argued that when a fixed deposit matures without renewal, the amount could attract the savings bank rate. The Division Bench rejected the defence. It noted that while banks were free under the RBI circular to determine rates on term deposits, that discretion was subject to the condition that there could be no discrimination between comparable deposits.
